title: YOU CAN WANT SOMETHING SO BADLY… AND STILL BE WALKING TOWARD YOUR OWN COLLAPSE
paragraphs:
YOU CAN WANT SOMETHING SO BADLY… AND STILL BE WALKING TOWARD YOUR OWN COLLAPSE
Desire is powerful. But when desire becomes louder than discernment, what feels irresistible today can become the very thing you beg God to rescue you from tomorrow.
There is a terrifying moment in the life of Samson that almost sounds harmless.
And when his parents question the wisdom of his desire, Samson does not stop to pray.
He does not ask whether what attracted his eyes was aligned with the heart of God.
“Get her for me; for she pleaseth me well.”
But the Hebrew underneath that statement makes the warning even sharper.
“For she is right in my eyes.”
One of the most dangerous sentences a human heart can speak.
“I have prayed, waited, listened, and tested this desire.”
And perhaps that is where some of our greatest collapses begin.
Not with a dramatic decision to destroy our lives.
Not with someone waking up one morning and saying, “Today I will ruin everything.”
A person you know you should release.
An opportunity that looks too good to question.
Money you feel you must have.
Attention you have become addicted to receiving.
A private conversation you know is becoming inappropriate.
A ministry position you want because being unseen has started hurting your ego.
A door you are trying to kick open because waiting on God has become unbearable.
And because you want it badly enough, you slowly begin confusing desire with direction.
Because desire can speak with incredible confidence.
Desire says, “Why would I feel this strongly if it were wrong?”
Desire says, “I’ll stop before it goes too far.”
And then one day you look around at the wreckage and wonder:
James gives an answer that is painfully uncomfortable.
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed.”
“Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.”
The Greek word translated “lust” in the King James Version is:
It refers to desire, longing, or craving. Depending on context, desire itself is not automatically sinful. The New Testament can use this family of words for desires that are not evil.
Christianity does not teach that having desires makes you wicked.
The danger is disordered desire—desire that refuses to remain underneath the authority of God.
James describes desire becoming a pathway.
Notice how rarely collapse begins at the collapse.
The affair begins before the hotel room.
The addiction begins before everything is lost.
The financial disaster begins before the account reaches zero.
The spiritual compromise begins before anyone else notices.
The betrayal begins before the secret is exposed.
The fall often begins quietly, in the private place where desire is allowed to negotiate with truth.
Discernment asks the question desire hates:
“Even though I want this… where will this lead me?”
Because somebody reading this is standing in front of something that feels beautiful right now.
And the real question may not be whether you want it.
“There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.”
The Hebrew word translated “way” is דֶּרֶךְ — derekh — a road, path, way, or course of life.
And the warning is frightening precisely because the road does not necessarily look deadly at the entrance.
If destruction always looked like destruction, temptation would be easy to recognize.
If adultery arrived looking like divorce papers, traumatized children, shattered trust, sleepless nights, and years of regret, fewer people would embrace it.
If pornography first appeared as emotional numbness, distorted intimacy, secrecy, shame, and bondage, fewer people would click.
If greed appeared carrying the anxiety it eventually produces, fewer people would worship money.
If bitterness showed you the person you would become after carrying it for ten years, forgiveness might suddenly look much more beautiful.
Sin survives by advertising the beginning while hiding the ending.
And this is why desire without discernment can lead to collapse.
One evening, David walked upon the roof of his palace.
And something happened between seeing and taking that changed the course of multiple lives.
He was told who she was.
“Is not this Bathsheba… the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”
That information should have been the boundary.
But desire had already begun speaking louder than discernment.
David tried to conceal what happened.
And when manipulation failed, concealment escalated.
Eventually Uriah—the very man David should have honored—was placed where battle would consume him.
David did not begin on the rooftop saying:
“I want to become an adulterer, deceive one of my loyal soldiers, orchestrate his death, dishonor God, and bring devastation into my household.”
That is what unchecked desire does.
Yesterday’s unthinkable act becomes tomorrow’s necessary cover-up.
And maybe that is what makes this message so uncomfortable.
Because some of us are asking God to bless something He has been warning us to leave.
But changing the label does not change the destination.
And perhaps you know exactly what this feels like.
You knew you should not send the message.
You knew you should not return.
You knew that relationship was pulling you farther from Christ.
But loneliness terrified you more than compromise.
But anger made you feel powerful.
You knew the Spirit was convicting you.
And then came the morning after.
The sick feeling inside your chest when the thing you desperately wanted finally gave you what it had been hiding.
But please do not stop reading here.
Because if this article ended with Samson, David, temptation, consequences, and collapse, it would not be the Gospel.
And Christianity is not ultimately the announcement that sinful people have ruined themselves.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for ruined people.
This is where scandal meets grace.
This is where the person who failed discovers that failure does not have to write the final chapter.
And when Nathan confronted him, David eventually stopped hiding behind royal power and confessed:
No pretending that being king placed him above judgment.
But listen to Nathan’s next words:
“The LORD also hath put away thy sin.”
That does not mean consequences disappeared.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves exactly how seriously God takes sin.
And ultimately the hope of sinners does not rest in David.
It rests in the Son of David.
The One who faced temptation without surrendering to sin.
The One who obeyed where we rebelled.
The One who remained righteous where we compromised.
The One who carried sin He never committed so guilty people could receive mercy they never earned.
At the cross, Jesus was not merely giving humanity motivational advice about making better decisions.
Christ “suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.”
“Fix yourself so Jesus will accept you.”
Turn from sin and come to the Savior who died and rose again.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Forgive whom you need to forgive.
And if necessary, walk away crying.
Better to grieve the loss of something God never intended for you than spend years grieving the destruction caused because you refused to let it go.
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
That is radically different from the gospel our desires preach.
Jesus teaches us to deny ourselves.
“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”
Maybe the deepest question is not:
“What does my desire want to make of me?”
Will this relationship make you more faithful to Christ or slowly normalize compromise?
Will this ambition make you a better servant or make everyone around you a tool for your success?
Will this opportunity require you to violate convictions you once begged God to strengthen?
Will this habit still look harmless when your children imitate it?
Will this secret survive the light?
Can you genuinely place this desire before Jesus and say:
“Lord, if this takes me away from You, I would rather lose it than lose intimacy with You”?
That prayer is terrifying when you desperately want something.
But surrender is where freedom begins.
And maybe tonight you do not need another sign.
Maybe you need courage to obey what God has already made clear.
Some doors are not blessings merely because they opened.
Some feelings are not instructions merely because they are intense.
Some opportunities are not assignments merely because they are available.
Some relationships are not ordained merely because the connection feels extraordinary.
Some desires must be surrendered precisely because Jesus is worth more.
Discernment is not living terrified of every decision.
It is learning to love Christ enough that truth receives the final word over appetite.
It is being able to say:
And perhaps those five words are exactly what someone reading this needs tonight.
More than the thing I once believed I could never surrender.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
Not because a comment saves you.
But sometimes putting a simple confession into words becomes a way of saying before other believers:
I do not want to keep pretending.
There is a human soul behind that screen.
Someone may be fighting a battle you survived.
Someone may be standing at the edge of a decision you already know ends painfully.
Someone may need the warning you wish somebody had given you.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity, purchases, or financial support.
Send it privately to the person who has been wrestling with compromise.
Supporting Gospel work should always be willing, never coerced.
But voluntary support can help Gospel Warrior keep creating, publishing, and sharing resources intended to point people toward Christ.
And whether or not you can financially support the ministry, you can still help.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is staring at something they desperately want.
They are convincing themselves that nobody will know.
They are interpreting intensity as permission.
And they cannot yet see where the road ends.
Maybe your share reaches them before the decision does.
Maybe your tag becomes the interruption.
Maybe your testimony reminds someone that repentance is still possible.
Maybe your comment tells another exhausted believer:
And maybe you are not reading this for somebody else at all.
Your opportunity to stop before desire becomes decision, decision becomes bondage, and bondage becomes collapse.
If so, do not merely feel convicted.
And surrender the thing you have been gripping so tightly.
Because the Savior who exposes our sin is also the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Your worst decision does not have greater authority than the blood of Jesus.
Your scandal does not have to become your identity.
Your collapse does not have to become your conclusion.
There is a new way forward in Christ.
And there is grace even for the person who ignored every warning and finally came home broken.
So remember this when desire starts whispering again:
What you refuse to surrender today may become the thing you desperately ask Jesus to rescue you from tomorrow—but what you place into His hands can no longer rule yours.
